title: Jacobson identities in an associative algebra of prime characteristic
statement: Let $F$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field], and let $A$ be an associative unital $F$-algebra, with no commutativity or finite-dimensionality assumption. Put $[a,b]=ab-ba$ and let $\operatorname{ad}(a):A\to A$ be the $F$-linear map $b\mapsto[a,b]$. For $1\le i<p$, define $s_i(a,b)\in A$ by declaring $i s_i(a,b)$ to be the coefficient of $t^{i-1}$ in $\operatorname{ad}(ta+b)^{p-1}(a)$ in $A[t]$, where $t$ is central. Then $\operatorname{ad}(a)^p=\operatorname{ad}(a^p)$ as endomorphisms of $A$, and $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}s_i(a,b)$ for all $a,b\in A$.

source.place: Section 10k, Proposition 10.38(a),(b), printed pp.205–206. The coefficient form of s_i is the expansion of the iterated-adjoint word definition just before the proposition.

proof.text: All integers in coefficients act through $F$. By [def-weil-field], every integer $k$ with $1\leq k<p$ is invertible in $F$: its image is nonzero because the characteristic is $p$. Direct cancellation in the defining integer factorial formulas gives $$k\binom pk=p\binom{p-1}{k-1},\qquad k\binom{p-1}{k}=(p-k)\binom{p-1}{k-1}.$$ Thus $\binom pk=0$ in $F$ for $0<k<p$. The second identity gives $\binom{p-1}{k}=-\binom{p-1}{k-1}$ in $F$, so induction from $\binom{p-1}0=1$ gives $\binom{p-1}{k}=(-1)^k$ for $0\leq k\leq p-1$. Also $(-1)^p=-1$ in $F$: for odd $p$ this is the usual parity identity, while for $p=2$ one has $-1=1$. These scalar equalities remain true when acting on any $F$-algebra, including the zero algebra.

source.place: Scalar binomial coefficients; elementary factorial calculations supplying the binomial congruences used on printed p.205

proof.text: For any associative unital $F$-algebra $B$ and $z\in B$, let $L_z(c)=zc$ and $R_z(c)=cz$. These are $F$-linear, and associativity gives $L_zR_z(c)=z(cz)=(zc)z=R_zL_z(c)$. Their powers satisfy $L_z^m(c)=z^mc$ and $R_z^m(c)=cz^m$, by induction from $m=0$. Apply [lem-sfb-commuting-binomial-expansion] in the associative ring $\operatorname{End}_F(B)$ to $L_z$ and $-R_z$; they commute by the preceding equality. Evaluate at $c$ and reindex using $\binom nj=\binom n{n-j}$ (the factorial formula) to obtain, for every $n\geq0$, $$\operatorname{ad}(z)^n(c)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j\binom nj z^{n-j}cz^j.$$ No two arbitrary elements of $B$ have been assumed to commute.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(a), printed p.205: commuting multiplication operators; full iterated-commutator expansion written out

proof.text: Apply the preceding expansion with $B=A$, $z=a$, $n=p$. All interior terms vanish by step 1. The two endpoint terms are $a^pc+(-1)^pca^p=a^pc-ca^p$. Consequently $\operatorname{ad}(a)^p(c)=\operatorname{ad}(a^p)(c)$ for every $c\in A$. Equality on every input is equality of the $F$-linear endomorphisms, proving the first clause.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(a), printed p.205, the two surviving endpoint terms

proof.text: Work now with finite polynomials $B=A[t]$, where $t$ commutes with every coefficient, and put $z=ta+b$. This is still an associative $F$-algebra. With $n=p-1$ and $c=a$, steps 1–2 give $$\operatorname{ad}(z)^{p-1}(a)=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}z^{p-1-j}az^j,$$ since $(-1)^j\binom{p-1}{j}=1$ in $F$. In particular no commutativity of $a$ and $b$ is used. This is the insertion sum that replaces the permutation counting in the proof of Proposition 10.38(b).

source.place: Proposition 10.38(b), printed pp.205–206; agent-supplied insertion-sum form of the same iterated-adjoint calculation

proof.text: Define $D(\sum_m c_mt^m)=\sum_{m\geq1}mc_mt^{m-1}$. It obeys $D(UV)=D(U)V+UD(V)$: for coefficients $u_r,v_s$, the coefficient of $t^q$ on the right is $\sum_{r+s=q+1}(r+s)u_rv_s$, precisely that on the left. The order $u_rv_s$ is unchanged. Since $Dz=a$, induction yields $$D(z^n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}z^{n-1-j}az^j\quad(n\geq1).$$ The base $n=1$ is $Dz=a$. For the step differentiate $z^{n+1}=z^nz$: multiply the insertion sum for $n$ on the right by $z$, then add $z^na$, giving exactly the $n+1$ insertion positions. Combining with step 4 gives $D(z^p)=\operatorname{ad}(z)^{p-1}(a)$.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(b), printed pp.205–206; agent-supplied finite polynomial coefficient proof of the product rule and insertion formula

proof.text: Set $Q(t)=(ta+b)^p-t^pa^p-b^p$. Expanding its finite product by distributivity shows that its constant coefficient is $b^p-b^p=0$ and its degree-$p$ coefficient is $a^p-a^p=0$, and that it has no terms of degree greater than $p$. Hence $Q(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}q_it^i$. Since $p=0$ in $F$, step 5 gives $$\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}i q_i t^{i-1}=DQ(t)=\operatorname{ad}(ta+b)^{p-1}(a).$$ By the coefficient definition in the item, the coefficient on the right at $t^{i-1}$ is $i s_i(a,b)$. Coefficient equality and the invertibility of $i\in F$ from step 1 give $q_i=s_i(a,b)$. Finally evaluation at the central scalar $t=1$ is multiplicative by the finite Cauchy product formula, so $Q(1)=\sum_i s_i(a,b)$ is exactly $(a+b)^p-a^p-b^p$. This proves the second clause by formal coefficient equality, without inferring polynomial equality from values in $F$.

source.place: Proposition 10.38(b), printed pp.205–206; agent-supplied coefficient argument for the exact coefficient normalization of the item

proof_origin.place: Section 10k, Proposition 10.38, printed pp.205–206. Part (a) follows the source. For (b), Q17 supplies a finite-polynomial derivative/coefficient version of its iterated-adjoint expansion, retaining the coefficient definition in the item rather than relying on the source’s word-index normalization.
